extracted.intended_audience: beat reporters / city-desk journalists covering meetings, conventions, anniversaries, fairs, and public officials
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for journalists on covering meetings, conventions, celebrations, fairs, and dealing with 'off the record' remarks; includes story structure, feature angles, practical reporting tactics, and ethics around confidential information. Geared to local/beat reporting for newspapers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Meeting-story block structure (preferred form)
rubrics_metrics.description: Lead, written for the casual reader; Block 2: Summary of the rest of the meeting; Block 3: Details of the lead material.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Two arrangements are shown; the first form (lead for casual reader, summary, then details) is preferable because it better highlights the whole meeting at the top of the story.

rubrics_metrics.name: Alternative longer-story block structure
rubrics_metrics.description: Second form: Block 1: Lead written for casual reader; Block 2: Elaboration of the lead; Block 3: Summary of the rest of the meeting.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When the longer story is used and speeches appear in later blocks, begin speech paragraphs with the speaker's name (e.g., 'Mr. Finch said in part') to prevent a rapid reader from missing the start of a new address.

rubrics_metrics.name: Begin speech paragraphs with speaker's name
rubrics_metrics.description: When transcribing speeches in longer stories, paragraphs that begin a new speech should start with the speaker's name rather than a quotation mark.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This prevents confusion where a reader might think a quotation continues the 'old' speech; examples show the clarity of 'Mr. Whipple said in part' versus a paragraph starting with a quote.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use volunteer informants but judge partisanship
rubrics_metrics.description: Expect volunteers eager to enlighten the reporter about 'true facts' but recognize they are almost always partisan and pushing a viewpoint.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Circulate among members to judge how much stock to take in what volunteers tell you; the more you circulate, the better you can assess their accuracy and bias.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cover selection and use of helpers for concurrent sessions
rubrics_metrics.description: When a meeting subdivides into several round tables or discussion groups, ask the in-charge or publicity official which gathering will probably be best and attend that one.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: To cover other sessions, conscript helpers: have the in-charge introduce you to chairmen of other meetings and arrange for them or their chosen delegates or secretaries to supply resumes/abstracts of what occurred.

rubrics_metrics.name: Run features/human-interest as separate stories
rubrics_metrics.description: Features or human-interest material from meetings often 'adorn' the reporter's work and are preferably run as separate stories rather than being forced into the main straight-news version.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A collection of tidbits or 'convention sidelights' can make a readable 'with' story; personal touches (e.g., notable attendees) are good as separate pieces.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mine officers' reports and statistics for stories
rubrics_metrics.description: Annual meeting reports (treasurer, secretary, president) often contain statistics and details that can yield good stories rather than being dismissed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If reports interest only members, roll them into a compact 'with' story; at times an analysis (e.g., long-term membership trends) will entice the casual reader—do the extra research to provide authoritative context.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not ignore other addresses because of a prize speaker
rubrics_metrics.description: Although the organization often reserves its best speaker for last, the reporter must not disregard the other addresses on the assumption that the last will cover everything.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Imported or prominent speakers are no guarantee of the best quotations; cover earlier talks as they may contain valuable material.

rubrics_metrics.name: Collect follow-up feature leads from meetings
rubrics_metrics.description: Reporters should draw from meetings at least half a dozen tips for feature or magazine-section stories to pursue later.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Listen for character slants, unusual claims, or human-interest hooks (e.g., 'the only man in this county who ever made a living as a patent attorney') that suggest future interviews or profiles.

rubrics_metrics.name: Anniversary/celebration story approach (theme and mood)
rubrics_metrics.description: For anniversaries or celebrations, immerse yourself in local history, isolate the underlying reason people attend, and create a theme that weaves through the story to produce a mood piece.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use selected quotations, trifles from conversations, and historical references to support the theme; avoid overdoing sentiment or 'gush'—balance member interest and casual reader appeal.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid: too skimpy specific information
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not write with only generalities; provide specific historical or factual details.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Without 'research' the reporter is forced into vague phrases (e.g., 'long and distinguished history') which members recognize as claptrap and resent—do background work to supply specifics.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid: gaudy adjectives and clichés
rubrics_metrics.description: A mood story crumbles if diction is inappropriately florid.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Keep diction consistently appropriate; spreading sentimentality or purple prose spoils the story.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid: failure to get into the spirit of the occasion
rubrics_metrics.description: Especially for anniversary chronicle pieces, failure to capture the occasion's spirit will disappoint the members who care deeply about it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Write to satisfy both members (who will read regardless) and casual readers; capitalize on participants' emotional overflow by giving them something to 'live over again.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid: lassitude and ennui
rubrics_metrics.description: Reporter fatigue or unwillingness to engage will prevent writing an absorbing account even when factual material exists.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not lean back and hope a short four-paragraph story suffices; energetic reporting and writing are needed for success.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid: failure to provide anything for the casual reader
rubrics_metrics.description: Few people outside the group care about the event, but many can be stimulated into interest if the reporter explains 'why' people attended and what made it noteworthy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Score on the other considerations (specifics, diction, spirit, energy) to make the story accessible to casual readers and not merely an in-group chronicle.

rubrics_metrics.name: Elements of a successful before-the-event 'plug' story
rubrics_metrics.description: Even a pre-event plug can be genuine if it presents background for non-specialists, gives focusing material (scale/what's scheduled), includes attention-grabbing details, uses direct quotations to humanize, provides authoritative specifics/dates, and develops a theme that may be stated at the end.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Structure paragraphs to answer 'why' and to show you observed closely; include an attention 'twitcher' (unusual parade entry), human quotes, and explicit dates to lend authority.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fair/county agricultural exhibit coverage
rubrics_metrics.description: Readers expect full lists of awards and contestants' results; contests and exhibitions deserve descriptions and summaries.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Put a high-up summary of the winners when long lists are cumbersome; describe contests in some detail, give compact accounts of outstanding exhibits, compare attendance with previous years, and coordinate with sports desk if events overlap.

rubrics_metrics.name: Off-the-record test: public/official vs private/personal
rubrics_metrics.description: The reporter's test for whether to honor 'off the record' is the distinction between public/official utterances and private/personal utterances.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Public statements made at open meetings or concerning official actions are on the record; private remarks at closed gatherings or clearly personal matters may be off the record and should be respected.

rubrics_metrics.name: Off-the-record: private/closed gatherings
rubrics_metrics.description: Remarks made at closed or members-only meetings (host-and-guest relationship) can legitimately be treated as off the record by participants.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the reporter attended only as a guest and the meeting was not open to the public, the speaker's 'off the record' designation should be honored.

rubrics_metrics.name: Off-the-record: public meetings are on the record
rubrics_metrics.description: When remarks are made at a public gathering open to anyone, declaring them 'off the record' does not make them so.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Speakers at public forums cannot later ask the newspaper to refrain from quoting them; the reporter may lawfully print what was said.

rubrics_metrics.name: Off-the-record: officials' personal matters vs official acts
rubrics_metrics.description: Personal matters of officials (e.g., inheritance plans) are private and can be off the record; official actions and statements about public business are matters of public concern and not off the record.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If an official volunteers personal information, it may be off the record; if asked about an official decision (e.g., whether the mayor will sign an order), the response is public and cannot be declared off the record to prevent publication.

rubrics_metrics.name: Off-the-record: matters not yet officially in public domain
rubrics_metrics.description: When an issue has not been formally made public (e.g., an auditor's hinted irregularities before official action), a reporter may be justified in suppressing such statements until they become official.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the subject is still hypothetical and not officially confirmed, a reporter may withhold publication to avoid wrongfully embarrassing sources.

rubrics_metrics.name: Clarify explicitly which remarks are off the record
rubrics_metrics.description: After a speaker says 'off the record,' the reporter should interrogate to determine exactly which statements are not usable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Failure to pin down which items were off the record has ruined many stories; confirm sentence-by-sentence or topic-by-topic if necessary.

rubrics_metrics.name: Salvaging off-the-record material via private interview/background
rubrics_metrics.description: Speakers may be willing to repeat material in private interviews without mentioning the meeting or club; this can salvage material otherwise unusable as direct quotes from the meeting.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ask if the source will make the same statements in a private interview 'with no mention of the Rotary Club' — if they agree, you may use the material under those terms.

rubrics_metrics.name: Guard against misuse of 'off the record' to silence public information
rubrics_metrics.description: Officials sometimes use 'off the record' to tie up information that should be publicly accessible; this misuse should be challenged.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If a public interest topic is being suppressed by repeated 'off the record' answers, break in and require the speaker to speak plainly or stop; the reporter is justified in refusing to accept such maneuvers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Protecting sources by anonymizing when necessary
rubrics_metrics.description: When a source (e.g., a city employee) can speak authoritatively but risks reprisal, the reporter may mask the story and omit the name, using formulations like 'sources close to city hall expected...'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use anonymous attribution to protect sources who are willing to speak but would suffer professional consequences if named; ensure accuracy and corroboration when granting anonymity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Handle unofficial censors (club members ejecting reporters)
rubrics_metrics.description: If private individuals attempt to bar a reporter from a meeting (e.g., 'We don't want any reporter here'), the reporter should verify with the club president or secretary whether he is welcome.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not be driven off by unofficial watchdogs; confirm the organization's official position before leaving; the city editor may have to decide whether continued ejection warrants a change in assignment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reporter discretion balancing relationships and public interest
rubrics_metrics.description: A reporter may accede to a public official's 'don't print it' request to preserve relationships or to obtain future access, but may ethically refuse when the story's worth outweighs the official's displeasure.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Weigh the value of the information and potential consequences; if printing will produce important public knowledge, the reporter is justified in publishing despite the request.
